title: The Ephesus riot (Acts 19:21–41)
hookLine: silversmiths start a riot for Artemis; a town clerk calms the crowd
tomorrow: a sermon runs past midnight. a young man is sitting in the window…

lines: GREAT IS DIANA, FOR TWO HOURS.
cards: A comment thread can go from zero to furious in one afternoon, and half the people in it couldn't tell you how it started. Ephesus, a packed theater: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians."

The crowd shouts it again and again, Acts says "about the space of two hours." Two of Paul's companions, Gaius and Aristarchus, have been dragged in. Paul wants to go in after them; his friends won't let him.
Then one man walks out in front of the crowd. Not an apostle. The town clerk.

teach.h: BY THIS CRAFT WE HAVE OUR WEALTH.
teach.b: Rewind to how it started. Demetrius, a silversmith who makes silver shrines of the goddess, calls the craftsmen together: "Sirs, ye know that by this craft we have our wealth."
Paul has been saying that gods made with hands are no gods, so their trade is in danger, and so is the goddess's honor. The King James calls her Diana; the Greek names her Artemis.
Tempers catch, and "the whole city was filled with confusion."

teach.h: THEY KNEW NOT WHY THEY CAME.
teach.b: Inside the theater, Acts gives a detail that's almost funny: "Some therefore cried one thing, and some another: for the assembly was confused; and the more part knew not wherefore they were come together."
Most of the crowd doesn't know why it's there. Now the town clerk. He quiets them, and makes a plain case.
Everyone knows this city honors its goddess. These men are "neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess."
If Demetrius has a complaint, the courts are open. "Ye ought to be quiet, and to do nothing rashly." Then "he dismissed the assembly."
Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: the peacemaker in this chapter isn't one of Paul's people at all.
Acts lets a city official, loyal to his own city's goddess, be the calm voice in the room, and tells it with respect.

how: Christians read the Ephesus riot in Acts 19 in church and Bible study; some teachers point to the town clerk when talking about keeping calm in conflict.

o: a theater crowd shouting for hours over a trade
a fire that destroyed a temple in Ephesus
a revolt of Roman soldiers against Paul

games.q: the riot in Ephesus — tap the pairs.
p: by this craft we have our wealth
most knew not why they had come

s: Paul calmed the riot with a speech
his friends kept him out. the town clerk quieted the crowd.
most of the crowd didn't know why they were there
the more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
the town clerk took Paul's side
he took no side: be quiet, do nothing rashly, and use the courts.

games.q: two dads start yelling in the stands at your little brother's basketball game, and people pull out phones. you're closest. what would the town clerk do?
o: lower the temperature, then point them to the ref and the rules.
work out which dad is right and back him up, loudly.
film it too, so there's a record of who started it.
games.why: the clerk quieted the crowd, said do nothing rashly, and sent the complaint to the courts. calm first, then the proper place.

practice: Sit or stand tall, and rest your hands open, palms down, the way someone signals a room to settle. Let your breathing slow until it's slower than a shout.
Stay there, and let one heated conversation from this week come to mind without joining it. A room gets calmer when even one person stops adding to the noise.

wordCard.voice: The Ephesus riot. Two hours of shouting in a theater, and a town clerk who quieted it.

orig.note: Greek: assembly. Acts 19:32 and 19:41 use it for the crowd in the theater.

carryVoice: Your line: be quiet, do nothing rashly. A town clerk said it, and a whole theater went home. See you tomorrow.
